fetched_contents.text: Laminated Object Manufacturing - an overview Chapters and Articles You might find these chapters and articles relevant to this topic. 2.6 Laminated object manufacturing Laminated object manufacturing (LOM) is one of the first commercially available additive manufacturing methods, which is based on layer-by-layer cutting and lamination of sheets or rolls of materials. Successive layers are cut precisely using a mechanical cutter or laser and are then bonded together (form-then-bond) or vice versa (bond-then-form). The form-then-bond method is particularly useful for thermal bonding of ceramics and metallic materials, which also facilitates the construction of internal features by removing excess materials before bonding. The excess materials after cutting are left for the support and after completion of the process, can be removed and recycled [28]. LOM can be used for a variety of materials such as polymer composites, ceramics, paper and metal-filled tapes. Post-processing such as high-temperature treatment may be required depending on the type of materials and desired properties. Ultrasonic additive manufacturing (UAM) is a new subclass of LOM which combines ultrasonic metal seam welding and CNC milling in the lamination process [29]. UAM is the only additive manufacturing method that is capable of construction of metal structures at low temperature [30,31]. LOM has been used in various industries such as paper manufacturing, foundry industries, electronics and smart structures. Smart structures are classified as structures (which can be multi-tasking) with a number of sensors and processors. Unlike conventional methods, UAM can specify cavities in the structure based on the integrated computer design for embedded electronic devices, sensors, pipes and other features. Electronic devices can be printed in the same lamination process of UAM using direct write technologies [28]. LOM can result in a reduction of tooling cost and manufacturing time, and is one of the best additive manufacturing methods for larger structures. However, LOM has inferior surface quality (without post-processing) and its dimensional accuracy is lower compared to the powder-bed methods. Also, removing the excess parts of laminates after formation of the object is time-consuming compared to the powder-bed methods. Therefore, it is not recommended for complex shapes. fetched_contents.text: Study of the key technologies of LOM for functional metal parts Abstract To address the problems associated with laminated object manufacturing (LOM) using sheet metal as a modeling material, an approach of cutting the sheet metals by a new LOM process and connecting them by diffusion welding technology is proposed. The conventional LOM process and the new LOM process are compared with reference to the theoretical manufacturing error. A slicing algorithm for the new LOM process has been deduced. The conclusions drawn from the experiments and analysis are shrinkage in the stack direction is small; atom diffusion between two joints occurs clearly and new grains form; the shear strength of the welding zone is above 100 MPa; the micro-hardness of the welding zone is almost the same as that of the substrate. The fabrication of sample part suggests that the new LOM process with diffusion welding could be a useful method for the rapid manufacturing of metal parts. Keywords Laminated object manufacturing ; Sheet metal ; Welding ; Dimensional accuracy Introduction After more than 10 years’ research and development, rapid prototyping/manufacturing (RP/M) has progressed greatly, since it began at the end of the 1980s, which has resulted in the development of a series of commercial RP/M systems. However, most of the modeling materials used in currently commercially available RP/M machines are resin, plastic, paper, or similar materials. The fabrication of parts is mainly for creating prototypes. To-date, almost none of the currently available RP technologies is suitable for the direct/rapid manufacture of functional mechanical parts. Therefore, one of the recent researches on RP/M has focused on the rapid manufacture of functional parts [1]. There have been a lot of researchers carrying out studies on the rapid manufacture of functional parts. For example, Murakami fabricated some high strength electrical composite resin models via a deposition modeling (FDM) process. The modeling material used was the mixture of thermoses resin, electrical materials and metal–ceramics powder [2]. Li manufactured parts for specific applications by embedding a sensor in the FDM models [3]. Nam produced sub-miniature ceramics parts for a micro gas turbine engine via the shape deposition manufacturing process [4]. Stephen tried to make metal matrix ceramics functional parts via the freeform powder modeling process [5]. Link made efforts in fabricating parts of carbon steel via a laser depositing process [6]. Since most mechanical parts are made of metal, it was recognized that laminated object manufacturing (LOM) of metal parts could be an effective methods for the manufacturing of metal functional parts, when using sheet metals as the modeling materials [7], [8]. Obikawa manufactured metal parts via the LOM process, in which 0.2 mm thick steel sheets, with their top and bottom surface coated with low-melting alloy, were used [9], [10]. Yamasaki manufactured the die for automobile body manufacturing, using 0.5 mm thick steel sheets via the LOM process [11]. There are, however, still a lot of problems existing in LOM using metal materials as the modeling materials: * (1) The modeling accuracy. It is apparent that the thinner are the slice sheets, the higher is the accuracy. Usually, the modeling materials used in current commercially available LOM processes is paper, resin sheets, etc., and the thickness of these kinds of sheets is in the range of 0.05–0.1 mm [12], [13], [14]. Considering the strength and efficiency of the model, current rapid manufacture for metal parts usually uses sheet metal of 0.2–0.5 mm thickness, but when employing such thickness of sheet metal, the part will be finished with low accuracy. * (2) Connecting technology for sheet metal. There have been such technologies for the connection of sheet metals as adhering them with low melting point alloy [9], [10], bolting them and then arc welding them [11], etc., but so far, these technologies have not brought the desired results to the LOM of using sheet metal as the modeling material. A new LOM process was proposed recently [15], [16]. Metal parts can be manufactured rapidly using 1.0 mm thick sheet metal by this process. Accuracy analysis demonstrated that the theoretical manufacturing error (called the theoretical error) of the process is almost equal to or even lower than that of the current LOM process of using 0.1 mm thick sheet. In [17], [18], an approach of connecting the sheet metals with diffusion welding technology was put forward and the feasibility of this approach was then demonstrated by experiment. As further research, a new LOM process with diffusion welding technology has been developed to manufacture metal parts rapidly. Mechanism of adhesion Adhesion processes are complex. Knowledge of the mechanism of adhesion has significant relevance to understand tissue adhesives and their use in clinical settings. However, there is no single theory to explain all the mechanisms due to the complexity adhesives present in terms of their nature and adhesion mechanism. At molecular level, adhesion can be summarized as mechanical interlocking, intermolecular bonding, chain entanglement, diffusion, and electrostatic binding (Fig. 1B) [29]. These molecular interactions can be physical or chemical in nature or both [15]. Intermolecular bonding Intermolecular bonding is the principal mechanism of adhesion and arises from intermolecular forces between the adhesive and the adherent on the intimate contact surface [30]. These intermolecular forces include primary chemical forces such as ionic, covalent, and metallic bonds and secondary physical forces in the form of dipole-dipole interactions, London dispersion, and van der Waals forces. Intermolecular bonding can be formed by primary and secondary forces or their combination [31]. Herein, the increase of the applied force until bond formation can enhance contact intimacy and contact area which leads to a strong adhesion [32]. Primary bonds present stronger adhesion compared to secondary bonds. Since these bonds are obtained from interactions between a specific chemical group on the adhesive molecule and a responsive chemical group on the substrate, specific surface pretreatment is often needed to achieve stronger interaction. Herein, adhesive can be modified chemically by incorporating specific functional groups into its chemical structure to generate chemical bonds between the adhesive and the adherent. Moreover, the surface of the adherent can be pretreated by using coupling agents or other adhesion promotor molecules [22,30,33]. Particularly, a covalent bond is the most common bond type among primary bonds. It mainly arises as an interaction between different functional groups such as activated ester, isocyanate, and aldehyde and primary amine of the chemical moieties on the surface of soft tissues through imine, Diels–Alder click chemistry, or Schiff-base reaction [12,28,34]. Secondary forces also play a considerable role in adhesion. Notably, when the interface between the adhesive and the adherent presents a great number of available sites for secondary bonding, these bonds can provide enhanced strong adhesion [28,33]. For instance, gecko inspired adhesives provide adhesion by non-covalent interactions through van der Waals and capillary forces [34]. Since adhesion is related to physicochemical properties of surface, it depends on physical properties of the adhesive surface and the response of adherent to this surface. In adhesion and physisorption, the van der Waals forces could arise from positively and negatively charged regions of the bonding molecules and keep together the surfaces of two materials owing to close proximity of their surfaces, as such the van der Waals interactions could become the main contributor to the adhesion [33,35]. Additionally, London dispersion forces are formed because of the interactive forces between temporary multipoles in molecules without permanent polarity [36]. There are different approaches to define adhesion between an adhesive and an adherent such as electron donor and acceptor interactions. Molecules having donor and acceptor properties result in the formation of molecular complexes to achieve stronger adhesion. For instance, Lewis acid and base could be electron donors and acceptors, respectively. Hydrogen bonds could be considered as donor and acceptor interactions [37]. Furthermore, wetting is strongly related to adhesion and in the adsorption theory, the formation of secondary forces is closely dependent on the wetting of adherents by adhesives. To obtain effective wetting, the surface energy of the adherent should be higher than the surface energy of the adhesive. Hence, surface pretreatment could be applied to enhance the surface energy of the adherent. It is known that wetting depends on mainly van der Waals forces, hydrogen bonding, and acid-base interactions [33]. Electrostatic bonding The electrostatic bonding mechanism is based on electrostatic interaction between oppositely-charged adhesive and adherent surfaces through a transfer of electrons at the interface [24]. The strength of electrostatic interaction depends on the charge density which can be altered by modulating the ionic content of surrounding media of the adhesive. Nevertheless, it may need a long time to provide the required charge concentration in the presence of insulator components due to the slow nature of charge build-up and limitation of available electrons [12,22]. Particularly, this mechanism is employed for incompatible materials such as a polymer, semiconductor, or metal. The contribution of electrostatic interaction has been found to be low compared to chemical bonding [24,38]. Meanwhile, it is also a possible mechanism for bioadhesion by sharing of electrons in some cases between the glycoproteins of the adherent and the bioadhesive material [16,39]. For instance, the interaction between mucin and chitosan happens due to electrostatic forces additionally supported by hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions [16]. Mechanical interlocking Mechanical interlocking is one of the oldest adhesion theories [40]. It involves penetration of the adhesive materials into pores and irregularities of the surface of the adherent. Herein, the trapped air on the interface is replaced with the adhesive and is followed by adherence of the material into microscopic roughness of the surface to provide complete binding. Step-by-step procedure of LOM

LOM follows a clear layer-by-layer workflow centered on cutting, stacking, and bonding successive layers of sheet material, with the process described in multiple sources as “layer by layer” or “successive” lamination [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5]. The basic sequence begins with a substrate or build platform, then adds a layer of sheet material, cuts it to shape, bonds it to the previous layer, and repeats this cycle until the object is formed [N2-R2][N2-R4][N2-R5].

Preparation of the substrate and build platform
The process starts with a prepared substrate and build platform. ScienceDirect describes LOM as using a stage with a material supply roll, and the first step is to feed a laminate of material onto the stage [N2-R2]. The build platform is also central to positioning and stability; LOM can be used with a variety of materials such as polymer composites, paper, ceramics, and metal-filled tapes [N1-F1][N3-R2]. The platform is usually moved down after each layer is cut and bonded, preparing it for the next layer [N1-F1]. In practical terms, the build platform must be flat, stable, and compatible with the sheet material being used, especially when handling metal sheets or adhesive-coated paper/plastic/metal [N3-R3][N3-R5].

Layer deposition and cutting sequence
The key operational step is layer deposition and cutting. The ScienceDirect overview states that successive layers are cut precisely using a mechanical cutter or laser, and the cut layers are then fused together [N2-R2]. Another source explains that the process uses a laser to cut a cross-section of the printed object from a sheet, after which the cut layer is bonded to the previous layer [N2-R4]. A technical description from ScienceDirect notes that the printing cycle includes rolling out a heat-activated sheet material, laminating it onto a substrate via the heat roller, forming the layer by laser-cutting the pattern, and cross-hatching the non-part area to be disposed to the waste roll [N1-F1]. This means the cutting sequence is not just a single shape cut; it is usually accompanied by cross-hatching or waste-area cutting that facilitates removal of excess material and supports the build cycle [N1-F1].

Support structure creation and removal
Support structures are an important part of the process, especially when the object has overhangs or complex geometry. One source notes that LOM can be used with support structures, and that after completion of the process, the excess parts of laminates can be removed and recycled [N1-F1]. Another source says that excess material after cutting is left for the support, and after completion of the process, it can be removed and recycled [N1-F1]. While the evidence here does not provide a detailed procedure for creating support structures specifically, it does establish that LOM includes support material and that its removal is a post-processing step [N1-F1][N4-R1]. In practice, this means support structures are built from the same or compatible sheet material, and they are later removed by hand or through mechanical means after the object is fully formed [N1-F1].

Post-processing steps after the build is complete
Post-processing is necessary to improve dimensional accuracy, surface finish, and overall quality. ScienceDirect notes that post-processing such as high-temperature treatment may be required depending on the type of materials and desired properties [N1-F1]. Another source says that post-processing is used to improve surface finish and dimensional accuracy of parts, and that various post-processing methods can affect dimensional accuracy [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Specific methods cited in the evidence include immersion, vapor treatment, polishing, and other finishing techniques [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5]. In the context of LOM, post-processing may include removing excess material, smoothing surfaces, and possibly heat treatment or other finishing operations to enhance the final object’s quality [N1-F1][N5-R3].

Overall procedure summary
In summary, the LOM step-by-step procedure is:
1. Prepare the substrate and build platform [N2-R2][N1-F1].
2. Feed a sheet material onto the stage or platform [N2-R2][N1-F1].
3. Cut the sheet material using a laser or mechanical cutter to form the desired layer [N2-R2][N2-R4][N1-F1].
4. Bond the cut layer to the previous layer [N2-R2][N2-R4][N1-F1].
5. Repeat the cycle, moving the platform down for the next layer [N1-F1].
6. Leave excess or support material for later removal [N1-F1].
7. After the object is formed, remove excess material and recycle it [N1-F1].
8. Perform post-processing to improve surface finish and dimensional accuracy [N5-R2][N5-R3].

The evidence is strongest for the basic sequence and the role of post-processing, but less detailed on the exact mechanical or software controls for cutting sequence and support-structure design [N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-R2].

Fundamental principles of LOM

LOM is a 3D printing process that builds objects layer by layer by cutting and bonding successive sheets of material [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The core difference from other additive manufacturing methods is that LOM does not typically melt or sinter the material in the way that powder-bed fusion or fused deposition modeling does; instead, it relies on sheet lamination and mechanical or adhesive bonding after cutting [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-R2]. This makes LOM a sheet-based additive manufacturing method, distinct from extrusion-based or light-curing systems [N1-F1][N1-R1].

Core concepts of layer-by-layer material bonding and substrate use
The central concept is layer-by-layer sheet cutting and stacking. ScienceDirect describes LOM as using successive layers that are cut precisely and then bonded together either by forming then bonding or bonding then forming [N1-F1]. It also says that successive layers are cut precisely using a mechanical cutter or laser and are then bonded together [N2-R2]. The ScienceDirect overview further states that the printing cycle includes rolling out a heat-activated sheet material, laminating it onto a substrate via the heat roller, forming the layer by laser-cutting the pattern, and cross-hatching the non-part area to be disposed to the waste roll [N1-F1]. This means the process is fundamentally sheet-based, with each layer built from a sheet of material that is cut and then attached to the previous layer [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-R2].

Substrate use is also central because the build platform is where the first layer is laminated and where subsequent layers are stacked [N1-F1]. The process can use a variety of substrates, including adhesive-coated paper, plastic, metal sheets, and composite sheets [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R5]. In the case of metal LOM, the source explicitly states that sheet metal can be used as the modeling material, and the process is intended for functional metal parts [N3-F2]. The use of a substrate is therefore not just a support structure; it is part of the lamination and bonding sequence [N1-F1].

Key advantages and limitations of the LOM approach
The main advantages of LOM include its ability to use a wide range of materials such as paper, plastic, metal, ceramics, and composite prepregs [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-F2]. It is also noted as a commercially available additive manufacturing method that can be used for larger structures, with reduced tooling cost and manufacturing time [N1-F1]. Another advantage is that it can be used with metal sheets and that it can produce metal parts with acceptable mechanical properties, including high shear strength and acceptable micro-hardness [N3-F2]. The overview also notes that LOM can be used in industries such as paper manufacturing, foundry industries, electronics, and smart structures [N1-F1].

The main limitations are inferior surface quality and lower dimensional accuracy compared to powder-bed methods [N1-F1]. The source explicitly states that LOM has poor to average finish and that its dimensional accuracy is lower compared to the powder-bed methods [N1-F1]. It also says that removing unwanted material from complex printed objects is time-consuming compared to powder-bed methods [N1-F1]. Another limitation is that LOM is not recommended for complex shapes because of the difficulty of removing excess parts [N1-F1]. Additionally, the source notes that LOM can result in a reduction of tooling cost and manufacturing time, but it is one of the best additive manufacturing methods for larger structures [N1-F1].

How process parameters influence bonding and quality
Process parameters influence bonding and quality because they affect how the layers are cut, bonded, and stacked. The ScienceDirect overview states that optimized laser power and scanning speed are key process parameters in the LOM technique [N7-R5]. Another source reports that an experimental investigation examined the influence of different process parameters on the vertical surfaces of LOM parts, measuring surface roughness [N7-R1]. A critical review also says that process parameters such as roller speed, roller temperature, laser cutting, and other variables affect the process [N7-R2][N7-R3]. A thermomechanical analysis notes that process parameters such as roller temperature, velocity, indentation, and chamber air temperature affect temperature and stress distributions [N7-R4]. These parameters are therefore directly linked to the quality of the final object.

In practical terms, process parameters influence bonding and quality by affecting:
- the precision of the cut [N7-R5],
- the adhesion between layers [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R4],
- the surface roughness and dimensional accuracy [N7-R1][N5-R2],
- the thermal and mechanical behavior of the material [N7-R4],
- and the overall efficiency and cycle time [N7-R2][N7-R3].

The evidence is strongest on the basic principle of sheet cutting and bonding, while the process-parameter details are more indirect and mostly indicate that they are important but not fully detailed in the provided sources [N1-R1][N1-F1][N7-R5].
node_outputs.N10:
Practical implementation and technical considerations

Equipment and tool selection for LOM
LOM equipment and tool selection depend on the process flow: feeding, cutting, bonding, and post-processing. The evidence shows that the process uses a supply roll, a stage, a mechanical cutter or laser, a heat roller, and a waste roll [N1-F1][N2-R2]. A laser is explicitly mentioned as the cutting tool in several sources, including the statement that the first step is the lamination of sheet material and the second step is the cutting of that material with a computer-controlled laser [N2-R4]. Another source says that successive layers are cut precisely using a mechanical cutter or laser [N2-R2]. This means that the choice of cutting tool is central to the process, with lasers being a common but not exclusive option [N2-R2][N2-R4].

For bonding, the sources indicate that layers are either bonded together after cutting or fused with heat or adhesive [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The ScienceDirect overview says that successive layers are cut and then bonded together [N1-F1], while another source states that the cut layers are then fused together using heat or adhesive [N1-R1]. This implies that bonding can be achieved through either thermal or adhesive means, depending on the material and the desired final properties [N1-R1][N1-F1].

The evidence also suggests the importance of a heat roller in the process, as ScienceDirect describes the printing cycle as involving rolling out a heat-activated sheet material and laminating it onto a substrate via the heat roller [N1-F1]. This means that the heat roller is part of the equipment selection and can affect material handling and lamination quality [N1-F1].

Process parameters that affect quality and speed
Several process parameters are identified as affecting quality and speed. The ScienceDirect overview states that optimized laser power and scanning speed are key process parameters in the LOM technique [N7-R5]. Another source reports that an experimental investigation examined the influence of different process parameters on the vertical surfaces of LOM parts, measuring surface roughness [N7-R1]. A critical review says that process parameters such as roller speed, roller temperature, laser cutting, and other variables affect the process [N7-R2][N7-R3]. A thermomechanical analysis notes that process parameters such as roller temperature, velocity, indentation, and chamber air temperature affect temperature and stress distributions [N7-R4].

These parameters influence the final object in several ways:
- laser power and scanning speed affect cutting quality and bonding [N7-R5].
- roller speed and temperature affect the lamination and adhesion process [N7-R2][N7-R3][N7-R4].
- chamber air temperature and base plate temperature affect thermal behavior and dimensional stability [N7-R3][N7-R4].
- indentation and other mechanical parameters affect stress and deformation [N7-R4].

Material compatibility and process constraints
Material compatibility is a major technical consideration. The sources indicate that LOM can use a variety of materials such as paper, plastics, metals, ceramics, and composite prepregs [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-F2]. However, the same sources also show that metal LOM has special constraints. One source states that metal sheet lamination, known as LOM, is a relatively inexpensive 3D printing technique for metallic and ceramic materials [N3-R1]. Another source says that metal sheet lamination is used for functional metal parts, and that metal parts can be manufactured rapidly using 1.0 mm thick sheet metal [N3-F2]. The study also notes that the modeling accuracy is mainly affected by the sheet thickness, with thinner sheets generally yielding higher accuracy [N3-F2].

Process constraints include:
- the thickness of the sheet material [N3-F2],
- the choice of bonding method (adhesive, heat, or diffusion welding) [N1-R1][N1-F1][N3-F2],
- the need for post-processing to improve surface finish and dimensional accuracy [N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R3],
- the time required to remove excess material and support structures [N1-F1],
- and the compatibility of the chosen material with the cutting and bonding process [N1-F1][N3-F2].

Dimensional accuracy and surface finish issues
Dimensional accuracy is a limitation of LOM. ScienceDirect explicitly states that LOM has poor to average finish and that its dimensional accuracy is lower compared to the powder-bed methods [N1-F1]. It also says that the accuracy of the z-axis is dependent on the thickness of the sheet used and the adhesion pressure [N1-F1]. The same source notes that the theoretical error in LOM arises from the step between each slice of sheet and the modeling surface, and that this step must be removed by finish processing [N1-F1].

Surface finish issues are addressed through post-processing. Multiple sources indicate that post-processing can improve surface finish and dimensional accuracy [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Specific post-processing methods cited in the evidence include immersion, vapor treatment, polishing, and other finishing techniques [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The evidence also suggests that post-processing is especially important for improving the final appearance and dimensional accuracy of LOM parts [N5-R2][N5-R3].

Overall, the technical considerations are clear: LOM requires careful selection of equipment and tools, including a cutting system, heat roller, and bonding method; it is sensitive to process parameters such as laser power, roller speed, and temperature; it is compatible with a wide range of materials but has special constraints when using metal or ceramic sheets; and it relies on post-processing to address surface finish and dimensional accuracy limitations [N1-F1][N2-R2][N7-R5][N5-R2][N5-R3].
node_outputs.N11:
Bonding, adhesion, and support-structure behavior

Mechanisms of layer adhesion and bonding
The evidence indicates that layer adhesion and bonding are central to LOM and that they can be achieved through several mechanisms. The ScienceDirect overview states that successive layers are cut and then bonded together either by forming then bonding or bonding then forming [N1-F1]. Another source says that the cut layers are then fused together using heat or adhesive [N1-R1]. This means that LOM bonding is not limited to a single mechanism; it can involve both thermal and adhesive bonding, depending on the material and the process configuration [N1-R1][N1-F1].

The mechanism of adhesion is also described in general adhesion theory. ScienceDirect states that adhesion can be summarized as mechanical interlocking, intermolecular bonding, chain entanglement, diffusion, and electrostatic binding [N4-R4]. A more detailed review explains that adhesion processes are complex and that adhesion can be formed by primary and secondary forces, including primary chemical forces such as ionic, covalent, and metallic bonds and secondary physical forces such as dipole-dipole interactions, London dispersion, and van der Waals forces [N4-F3]. The review also notes that primary bonds are stronger than secondary bonds, and that specific surface pretreatment is often needed to achieve stronger interaction [N4-F3]. It further states that covalent bonds are the most common primary bonds and that adhesion can be modified chemically by incorporating functional groups or using coupling agents and adhesion promoters [N4-F3].

Support-structure adhesion issues and design considerations
Support-structure adhesion issues are relevant in LOM, even though the evidence here is more general than LOM-specific. One source discusses support structure adhesion issues in 3D printing and notes that support structures may not adhere properly [N4-R1]. Another source describes first-layer adhesion issues for support material, indicating that support material can fail to adhere at the first layer [N4-R2]. These sources suggest that support-structure adhesion is a common concern in additive manufacturing, but they do not provide a detailed LOM-specific design methodology.

In the context of LOM, support structures are created from the same or compatible sheet material and are later removed [N1-F1]. The evidence indicates that excess material after cutting is left for the support, and after completion of the process, it can be removed and recycled [N1-F1]. This implies that support structures are part of the build process and are designed to hold up overhanging or complex regions during printing [N1-F1]. However, the provided evidence does not detail how they are specifically designed or how adhesion between the support and the object is optimized [N4-R1][N4-R2].

Conditions that cause delamination or poor bonding
Delamination or poor bonding can occur when the adhesion conditions are not favorable. The adhesion review states that adhesion can fail if the interface is not intimate enough, if the contact area is insufficient, or if the bond is not strong enough [N4-F3]. It also notes that wetting is strongly related to adhesion and that the surface energy of the adherent should be higher than the surface energy of the adhesive for effective wetting [N4-F3]. Poor bonding may therefore result from:
- insufficient intimacy or contact area,
- inadequate wetting,
- weak primary or secondary bonding,
- insufficient surface pretreatment,
- incorrect chemical or physical compatibility,
- or unfavorable environmental conditions such as temperature and pressure [N4-F3][N4-R4].

How adhesion affects dimensional accuracy
Adhesion directly affects dimensional accuracy because poor bonding can create steps or uneven interfaces between layers. The ScienceDirect overview states that the theoretical error in LOM arises from the step between each slice of sheet and the modeling surface, and that this step must be removed by finish processing [N1-F1]. It also notes that dimensional accuracy is lower compared to powder-bed methods and that the z-axis accuracy is dependent on the sheet thickness and adhesion pressure [N1-F1]. This means that weak or uneven bonding can create visible steps or inaccuracies in the z-direction.

The evidence also suggests that surface roughness and dimensional accuracy are affected by process parameters such as roller speed, roller temperature, and laser cutting [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3]. Since these parameters influence how layers are bonded and stacked, they indirectly affect dimensional accuracy [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3]. In other words, better adhesion and better control of the bonding process can improve dimensional accuracy, while poor adhesion and inconsistent bonding can degrade it [N1-F1][N7-R1].

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that LOM relies on layer-by-layer bonding through thermal or adhesive means, that adhesion is governed by mechanical interlocking, intermolecular bonding, and other molecular mechanisms, and that support-structure adhesion is a practical concern that can affect the overall quality of the build [N1-R1][N1-F1][N4-R4][N4-F3]. Poor bonding can cause delamination or steps, and weak adhesion can reduce dimensional accuracy [N1-F1][N4-F3].

# Laminated Object Manufacturing (LOM): Fundamental Principles and Step-by-Step Procedures

Laminated Object Manufacturing, or LOM, is a 3D printing process that builds objects layer by layer by cutting and bonding successive sheets of material [N1-R1][N1-F1]. It is one of the earliest commercially available additive manufacturing methods, and its defining feature is that it is sheet-based rather than melt-based, powder-based, or extrusion-based. In LOM, successive layers are cut precisely and then bonded together either by forming then bonding or bonding then forming [N1-F1]. The process can use a wide range of materials, including paper, plastic, metal, ceramics, and composite sheets [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R5]. This makes LOM distinct from other additive manufacturing methods in that it does not typically require melting or sintering the material in the same way as powder-bed fusion or fused deposition modeling [N1-R1][N1-F1].

## 1. Fundamental principles of LOM

### What LOM is and how it differs from other additive manufacturing methods
LOM is a 3D printing process that uses a layer-by-layer workflow: feed a sheet material onto a stage or platform, cut it to shape, bond it to the previous layer, and repeat until the object is formed [N1-F1][N2-R2]. The core difference from other additive manufacturing methods is that LOM relies on sheet lamination and bonding after cutting, rather than on melting, sintering, or extruding the material [N1-R1][N1-F1]. It is also sheet-based, meaning the process is centered on feeding, cutting, and stacking successive layers of sheet material [N1-F1][N2-R2]. This makes it fundamentally different from extrusion-based or light-curing systems, and it is often described as one of the first commercially available additive manufacturing methods [N1-F1].

### Core concepts of layer-by-layer material bonding and substrate use
LOM is built around successive layers that are cut precisely and then bonded together [N1-F1]. The process can use a variety of substrates, including adhesive-coated paper, plastic, metal sheets, and composite sheets [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R5]. The build platform is central to the process because the first layer is laminated onto a substrate, and subsequent layers are stacked upon it [N1-F1]. In some configurations, the platform is moved down after each layer is cut and bonded, preparing it for the next layer [N1-F1]. This means the substrate is not only a support surface; it is part of the lamination and bonding sequence [N1-F1].

### Key advantages and limitations of the LOM approach
The main advantages of LOM are:
- the ability to use a wide range of materials, including paper, plastic, metal, ceramics, and composite sheets [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-F2],
- reduced tooling cost and manufacturing time [N1-F1],
- the ability to produce larger structures [N1-F1],
- and the potential for functional metal parts when metal sheet lamination is used [N3-F2].

The main limitations are:
- inferior surface quality and lower dimensional accuracy compared to powder-bed methods [N1-F1],
- poor to average finish in the source descriptions [N1-F1],
- and the difficulty of removing unwanted material from complex printed objects [N1-F1].

### How process parameters influence bonding and quality
Process parameters are central to the quality and behavior of the LOM process. The evidence indicates that optimized laser power and scanning speed are key process parameters in LOM [N7-R5]. An experimental investigation also examined the influence of different process parameters on the vertical surfaces of LOM parts, measuring surface roughness [N7-R1]. A critical review states that process parameters such as roller speed, roller temperature, laser cutting, and other variables affect the process [N7-R2][N7-R3]. A thermomechanical analysis notes that process parameters such as roller temperature, velocity, indentation, and chamber air temperature affect temperature and stress distributions [N7-R4].

These parameters influence bonding and quality in several ways:
- they affect the precision of the cut [N7-R5],
- they affect the adhesion between layers [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R4],
- they affect surface roughness and dimensional accuracy [N7-R1][N5-R2],
- and they affect the thermal and mechanical behavior of the material [N7-R4].

In other words, better control of process parameters can improve dimensional accuracy and bonding quality, while poor parameter control can degrade them [N1-F1][N7-R1][N7-R5].

## 2. Step-by-step procedure of LOM

LOM follows a clear layer-by-layer workflow centered on cutting, stacking, and bonding successive layers of sheet material [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5]. The process is described in multiple sources as “layer by layer” or “successive” lamination [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5]. The basic sequence is:
1. prepare the substrate and build platform,
2. feed a sheet material onto the stage or platform,
3. cut the sheet material using a laser or mechanical cutter to form the desired layer,
4. bond the cut layer to the previous layer,
5. repeat the cycle,
6. leave excess or support material for later removal,
7. after the object is formed, remove excess material and recycle it,
8. perform post-processing to improve surface finish and dimensional accuracy [N2-R2][N2-R4][N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

### Preparation of the substrate and build platform
The process begins with a prepared substrate and build platform. ScienceDirect describes LOM as using a stage with a material supply roll, and the first step is to feed a laminate of material onto the stage [N2-R2]. The build platform is also central to positioning and stability; LOM can be used with a variety of materials such as polymer composites, paper, ceramics, and metal-filled tapes [N1-F1][N3-R2]. The platform is usually moved down after each layer is cut and bonded, preparing it for the next layer [N1-F1]. In practical terms, the build platform must be flat, stable, and compatible with the sheet material being used, especially when handling metal sheets or adhesive-coated paper/plastic/metal [N3-R3][N3-R5].

### Layer deposition and cutting sequence
The key operational step is layer deposition and cutting. The ScienceDirect overview states that successive layers are cut precisely using a mechanical cutter or laser, and the cut layers are then bonded together [N2-R2]. Another source explains that the process uses a laser to cut a cross-section of the printed object from a sheet, after which the cut layer is bonded to the previous layer [N2-R4]. A technical description from ScienceDirect notes that the printing cycle includes rolling out a heat-activated sheet material, laminating it onto a substrate via the heat roller, forming the layer by laser-cutting the pattern, and cross-hatching the non-part area to be disposed to the waste roll [N1-F1]. This means the cutting sequence is not just a single shape cut; it is usually accompanied by cross-hatching or waste-area cutting that facilitates removal of excess material and supports the build cycle [N1-F1].

### Support structure creation and removal
Support structures are an important part of the process, especially when the object has overhangs or complex geometry. One source notes that LOM can be used with support structures, and that after completion of the process, the excess parts of laminates can be removed and recycled [N1-F1]. Another source says that excess material after cutting is left for the support, and after completion of the process, it can be removed and recycled [N1-F1]. While the evidence here does not provide a detailed procedure for creating support structures specifically, it does establish that LOM includes support material and that its removal is a post-processing step [N1-F1][N4-R1]. In practice, this means support structures are built from the same or compatible sheet material, and they are later removed by hand or through mechanical means after the object is fully formed [N1-F1].

### Post-processing steps after the build is complete
Post-processing is necessary to improve dimensional accuracy, surface finish, and overall quality. ScienceDirect notes that post-processing such as high-temperature treatment may be required depending on the type of materials and desired properties [N1-F1]. Another source says that post-processing is used to improve surface finish and dimensional accuracy of parts, and that various post-processing methods can affect dimensional accuracy [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Specific methods cited in the evidence include immersion, vapor treatment, polishing, and other finishing techniques [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5]. In the context of LOM, post-processing may include removing excess material, smoothing surfaces, and possibly heat treatment or other finishing operations to enhance the final object’s quality [N1-F1][N5-R3].

## 3. Practical implementation and technical considerations

### Equipment and tool selection for LOM
LOM equipment and tool selection depend on the process flow: feeding, cutting, bonding, and post-processing. The evidence shows that the process uses a supply roll, a stage, a mechanical cutter or laser, a heat roller, and a waste roll [N1-F1][N2-R2]. A laser is explicitly mentioned as the cutting tool in several sources, including the statement that the first step is the lamination of sheet material and the second step is the cutting of that material with a computer-controlled laser [N2-R4]. Another source says that successive layers are cut precisely using a mechanical cutter or laser [N2-R2]. This means that the choice of cutting tool is central to the process, with lasers being a common but not exclusive option [N2-R2][N2-R4].

For bonding, the sources indicate that layers are either bonded together after cutting or fused with heat or adhesive [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The ScienceDirect overview says that successive layers are cut and then bonded together [N1-F1], while another source states that the cut layers are then fused together using heat or adhesive [N1-R1]. This implies that bonding can be achieved through either thermal or adhesive means, depending on the material and the desired final properties [N1-R1][N1-F1].

The evidence also suggests the importance of a heat roller in the process, as ScienceDirect describes the printing cycle as involving rolling out a heat-activated sheet material and laminating it onto a substrate via the heat roller [N1-F1]. This means that the heat roller is part of the equipment selection and can affect material handling and lamination quality [N1-F1].

### Process parameters that affect quality and speed
Several process parameters are identified as affecting quality and speed. The ScienceDirect overview states that optimized laser power and scanning speed are key process parameters in the LOM technique [N7-R5]. Another source reports that an experimental investigation examined the influence of different process parameters on the vertical surfaces of LOM parts, measuring surface roughness [N7-R1]. A critical review says that process parameters such as roller speed, roller temperature, laser cutting, and other variables affect the process [N7-R2][N7-R3]. A thermomechanical analysis notes that process parameters such as roller temperature, velocity, indentation, and chamber air temperature affect temperature and stress distributions [N7-R4].

These parameters influence the final object in several ways:
- laser power and scanning speed affect cutting quality and bonding [N7-R5],
- roller speed and temperature affect the lamination and adhesion process [N7-R2][N7-R3][N7-R4],
- chamber air temperature and base plate temperature affect thermal behavior and dimensional stability [N7-R3][N7-R4],
- indentation and other mechanical parameters affect stress and deformation [N7-R4].

### Material compatibility and process constraints
Material compatibility is a major technical consideration. The sources indicate that LOM can use a variety of materials such as paper, plastics, metals, ceramics, and composite prepregs [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-F2]. However, the same sources also show that metal LOM has special constraints. One source states that metal sheet lamination, known as LOM, is a relatively inexpensive 3D printing technique for metallic and ceramic materials [N3-R1]. Another source says that metal sheet lamination is used for functional metal parts, and that metal parts can be manufactured rapidly using 1.0 mm thick sheet metal [N3-F2]. The study also notes that the modeling accuracy is mainly affected by the sheet thickness, with thinner sheets generally yielding higher accuracy [N3-F2].

Process constraints include:
- the thickness of the sheet material [N3-F2],
- the choice of bonding method (adhesive, heat, or diffusion welding) [N1-R1][N1-F1][N3-F2],
- the need for post-processing to improve surface finish and dimensional accuracy [N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R3],
- the time required to remove excess material and support structures [N1-F1],
- and the compatibility of the chosen material with the cutting and bonding process [N1-F1][N3-F2].

### Dimensional accuracy and surface finish issues
Dimensional accuracy is a limitation of LOM. ScienceDirect explicitly states that LOM has poor to average finish and that its dimensional accuracy is lower compared to the powder-bed methods [N1-F1]. It also says that the accuracy of the z-axis is dependent on the thickness of the sheet used and the adhesion pressure [N1-F1]. The same source notes that the theoretical error in LOM arises from the step between each slice of sheet and the modeling surface, and that this step must be removed by finish processing [N1-F1].

Surface finish issues are addressed through post-processing. Multiple sources indicate that post-processing can improve surface finish and dimensional accuracy [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Specific post-processing methods cited in the evidence include immersion, vapor treatment, polishing, and other finishing techniques [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The evidence also suggests that post-processing is especially important for improving the final appearance and dimensional accuracy of LOM parts [N5-R2][N5-R3].

## 4. Bonding, adhesion, and support-structure behavior

### Mechanisms of layer adhesion and bonding
The evidence indicates that layer adhesion and bonding are central to LOM and that they can be achieved through several mechanisms. The ScienceDirect overview states that successive layers are cut and then bonded together either by forming then bonding or bonding then forming [N1-F1]. Another source says that the cut layers are then fused together using heat or adhesive [N1-R1]. This means that LOM bonding is not limited to a single mechanism; it can involve both thermal and adhesive bonding, depending on the material and the process configuration [N1-R1][N1-F1].

The mechanism of adhesion is also described in general adhesion theory. ScienceDirect states that adhesion can be summarized as mechanical interlocking, intermolecular bonding, chain entanglement, diffusion, and electrostatic binding [N4-R4]. A more detailed review explains that adhesion processes are complex and that adhesion can be formed by primary and secondary forces, including primary chemical forces such as ionic, covalent, and metallic bonds and secondary physical forces such as dipole-dipole interactions, London dispersion, and van der Waals forces [N4-F3]. The review also notes that primary bonds are stronger than secondary bonds, and that specific surface pretreatment is often needed to achieve stronger interaction [N4-F3]. It further states that covalent bonds are the most common primary bonds and that adhesion can be modified chemically by incorporating functional groups or using coupling agents and adhesion promoters [N4-F3].

### Support-structure adhesion issues and design considerations
Support-structure adhesion issues are relevant in LOM, even though the evidence here is more general than LOM-specific. One source discusses support structure adhesion issues in 3D printing and notes that support structures may not adhere properly [N4-R1]. Another source describes first-layer adhesion issues for support material, indicating that support material can fail to adhere at the first layer [N4-R2]. These sources suggest that support-structure adhesion is a common concern in additive manufacturing, but they do not provide a detailed LOM-specific design methodology.

In the context of LOM, support structures are created from the same or compatible sheet material and are later removed [N1-F1]. The evidence indicates that excess material after cutting is left for the support, and after completion of the process, it can be removed and recycled [N1-F1]. This implies that support structures are part of the build process and are designed to hold up overhanging or complex regions during printing [N1-F1]. However, the provided evidence does not detail how they are specifically designed or how adhesion between the support and the object is optimized [N4-R1][N4-R2].

### Conditions that cause delamination or poor bonding
Delamination or poor bonding can occur when the adhesion conditions are not favorable. The adhesion review states that adhesion can fail if the interface is not intimate enough, if the contact area is insufficient, or if the bond is not strong enough [N4-F3]. It also notes that wetting is strongly related to adhesion and that the surface energy of the adherent should be higher than the surface energy of the adhesive for effective wetting [N4-F3]. Poor bonding may therefore result from:
- insufficient intimacy or contact area,
- inadequate wetting,
- weak primary or secondary bonding,
- insufficient surface pretreatment,
- incorrect chemical or physical compatibility,
- or unfavorable environmental conditions such as temperature and pressure [N4-F3][N4-R4].

### How adhesion affects dimensional accuracy
Adhesion directly affects dimensional accuracy because poor bonding can create steps or uneven interfaces between layers. The ScienceDirect overview states that the theoretical error in LOM arises from the step between each slice of sheet and the modeling surface, and that this step must be removed by finish processing [N1-F1]. It also notes that dimensional accuracy is lower compared to powder-bed methods and that the z-axis accuracy is dependent on the sheet thickness and adhesion pressure [N1-F1]. This means that weak or uneven bonding can create visible steps or inaccuracies in the z-direction.

The evidence also suggests that surface roughness and dimensional accuracy are affected by process parameters such as roller speed, roller temperature, and laser cutting [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3]. Since these parameters influence how layers are bonded and stacked, they indirectly affect dimensional accuracy [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3]. In other words, better adhesion and better control of the bonding process can improve dimensional accuracy, while poor adhesion and inconsistent bonding can degrade it [N1-F1][N7-R1].

## 5. Integrated conclusion

Overall, LOM is a layered additive manufacturing process that builds objects by cutting and bonding successive sheets of material [N1-R1][N1-F1]. Its fundamental principles are:
- sheet-based layer-by-layer construction,
- use of adhesive or thermal bonding after cutting,
- substrate use as part of the lamination sequence,
- and a wide range of compatible materials such as paper, plastic, metal, ceramics, and composites [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

The step-by-step procedure is:
1. prepare the substrate and build platform,
2. feed a sheet material onto the stage or platform,
3. cut the sheet material using a laser or mechanical cutter to form the desired layer,
4. bond the cut layer to the previous layer,
5. repeat the cycle,
6. leave excess or support material for later removal,
7. after the object is formed, remove excess material and recycle it,
8. perform post-processing to improve surface finish and dimensional accuracy [N2-R2][N2-R4][N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

The practical considerations are:
- equipment selection should include a cutting system, heat roller, and bonding method,
- process parameters such as laser power, roller speed, temperature, and chamber air temperature affect quality and speed,
- material compatibility is important, especially for metal and ceramic sheets,
- post-processing is needed to address dimensional accuracy and surface finish,
- and adhesion behavior is central to bonding quality and dimensional accuracy [N1-F1][N2-R2][N7-R5][N7-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

In summary, LOM is a valuable but limited additive manufacturing method that excels in large-scale, rapid prototyping and functional metal applications, but it requires careful attention to bonding, material selection, process parameters, and post-processing to achieve acceptable quality and dimensional accuracy [N1-F1][N3-F2][N7-R5].

Step-by-step procedure of LOM

LOM follows a clear layer-by-layer workflow centered on cutting, stacking, and bonding successive layers of sheet material, with the process described in multiple sources as “layer by layer” or “successive” lamination [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5]. The basic sequence begins with a substrate or build platform, then adds a layer of sheet material, cuts it to shape, bonds it to the previous layer, and repeats this cycle until the object is formed [N2-R2][N2-R4][N2-R5].

Preparation of the substrate and build platform
The process starts with a prepared substrate and build platform. ScienceDirect describes LOM as using a stage with a material supply roll, and the first step is to feed a laminate of material onto the stage [N2-R2]. The build platform is also central to positioning and stability; LOM can be used with a variety of materials such as polymer composites, paper, ceramics, and metal-filled tapes [N1-F1][N3-R2]. The platform is usually moved down after each layer is cut and bonded, preparing it for the next layer [N1-F1]. In practical terms, the build platform must be flat, stable, and compatible with the sheet material being used, especially when handling metal sheets or adhesive-coated paper/plastic/metal [N3-R3][N3-R5].

Layer deposition and cutting sequence
The key operational step is layer deposition and cutting. The ScienceDirect overview states that successive layers are cut precisely using a mechanical cutter or laser, and the cut layers are then fused together [N2-R2]. Another source explains that the process uses a laser to cut a cross-section of the printed object from a sheet, after which the cut layer is bonded to the previous layer [N2-R4]. A technical description from ScienceDirect notes that the printing cycle includes rolling out a heat-activated sheet material, laminating it onto a substrate via the heat roller, forming the layer by laser-cutting the pattern, and cross-hatching the non-part area to be disposed to the waste roll [N1-F1]. This means the cutting sequence is not just a single shape cut; it is usually accompanied by cross-hatching or waste-area cutting that facilitates removal of excess material and supports the build cycle [N1-F1].

Support structure creation and removal
Support structures are an important part of the process, especially when the object has overhangs or complex geometry. One source notes that LOM can be used with support structures, and that after completion of the process, the excess parts of laminates can be removed and recycled [N1-F1]. Another source says that excess material after cutting is left for the support, and after completion of the process, it can be removed and recycled [N1-F1]. While the evidence here does not provide a detailed procedure for creating support structures specifically, it does establish that LOM includes support material and that its removal is a post-processing step [N1-F1][N4-R1]. In practice, this means support structures are built from the same or compatible sheet material, and they are later removed by hand or through mechanical means after the object is fully formed [N1-F1].

Post-processing steps after the build is complete
Post-processing is necessary to improve dimensional accuracy, surface finish, and overall quality. ScienceDirect notes that post-processing such as high-temperature treatment may be required depending on the type of materials and desired properties [N1-F1]. Another source says that post-processing is used to improve surface finish and dimensional accuracy of parts, and that various post-processing methods can affect dimensional accuracy [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Specific methods cited in the evidence include immersion, vapor treatment, polishing, and other finishing techniques [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5]. In the context of LOM, post-processing may include removing excess material, smoothing surfaces, and possibly heat treatment or other finishing operations to enhance the final object’s quality [N1-F1][N5-R3].

Overall procedure summary
In summary, the LOM step-by-step procedure is:
1. Prepare the substrate and build platform [N2-R2][N1-F1].
2. Feed a sheet material onto the stage or platform [N2-R2][N1-F1].
3. Cut the sheet material using a laser or mechanical cutter to form the desired layer [N2-R2][N2-R4][N1-F1].
4. Bond the cut layer to the previous layer [N2-R2][N2-R4][N1-F1].
5. Repeat the cycle, moving the platform down for the next layer [N1-F1].
6. Leave excess or support material for later removal [N1-F1].
7. After the object is formed, remove excess material and recycle it [N1-F1].
8. Perform post-processing to improve surface finish and dimensional accuracy [N5-R2][N5-R3].

The evidence is strongest for the basic sequence and the role of post-processing, but less detailed on the exact mechanical or software controls for cutting sequence and support-structure design [N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-R2].

Fundamental principles of LOM

LOM is a 3D printing process that builds objects layer by layer by cutting and bonding successive sheets of material [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The core difference from other additive manufacturing methods is that LOM does not typically melt or sinter the material in the way that powder-bed fusion or fused deposition modeling does; instead, it relies on sheet lamination and mechanical or adhesive bonding after cutting [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-R2]. This makes LOM a sheet-based additive manufacturing method, distinct from extrusion-based or light-curing systems [N1-F1][N1-R1].

Core concepts of layer-by-layer material bonding and substrate use
The central concept is layer-by-layer sheet cutting and stacking. ScienceDirect describes LOM as using successive layers that are cut precisely and then bonded together either by forming then bonding or bonding then forming [N1-F1]. It also says that successive layers are cut precisely using a mechanical cutter or laser and are then bonded together [N2-R2]. The ScienceDirect overview further states that the printing cycle includes rolling out a heat-activated sheet material, laminating it onto a substrate via the heat roller, forming the layer by laser-cutting the pattern, and cross-hatching the non-part area to be disposed to the waste roll [N1-F1]. This means the process is fundamentally sheet-based, with each layer built from a sheet of material that is cut and then attached to the previous layer [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-R2].

Substrate use is also central because the build platform is where the first layer is laminated and where subsequent layers are stacked [N1-F1]. The process can use a variety of substrates, including adhesive-coated paper, plastic, metal sheets, and composite sheets [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R5]. In the case of metal LOM, the source explicitly states that sheet metal can be used as the modeling material, and the process is intended for functional metal parts [N3-F2]. The use of a substrate is therefore not just a support structure; it is part of the lamination and bonding sequence [N1-F1].

Key advantages and limitations of the LOM approach
The main advantages of LOM include its ability to use a wide range of materials such as paper, plastic, metal, ceramics, and composite prepregs [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-F2]. It is also noted as a commercially available additive manufacturing method that can be used for larger structures, with reduced tooling cost and manufacturing time [N1-F1]. Another advantage is that it can be used with metal sheets and that it can produce metal parts with acceptable mechanical properties, including high shear strength and acceptable micro-hardness [N3-F2]. The overview also notes that LOM can be used in industries such as paper manufacturing, foundry industries, electronics, and smart structures [N1-F1].

The main limitations are inferior surface quality and lower dimensional accuracy compared to powder-bed methods [N1-F1]. The source explicitly states that LOM has poor to average finish and that its dimensional accuracy is lower compared to the powder-bed methods [N1-F1]. It also says that removing unwanted material from complex printed objects is time-consuming compared to powder-bed methods [N1-F1]. Another limitation is that LOM is not recommended for complex shapes because of the difficulty of removing excess parts [N1-F1]. Additionally, the source notes that LOM can result in a reduction of tooling cost and manufacturing time, but it is one of the best additive manufacturing methods for larger structures [N1-F1].

How process parameters influence bonding and quality
Process parameters influence bonding and quality because they affect how the layers are cut, bonded, and stacked. The ScienceDirect overview states that optimized laser power and scanning speed are key process parameters in the LOM technique [N7-R5]. Another source reports that an experimental investigation examined the influence of different process parameters on the vertical surfaces of LOM parts, measuring surface roughness [N7-R1]. A critical review also says that process parameters such as roller speed, roller temperature, laser cutting, and other variables affect the process [N7-R2][N7-R3]. A thermomechanical analysis notes that process parameters such as roller temperature, velocity, indentation, and chamber air temperature affect temperature and stress distributions [N7-R4]. These parameters are therefore directly linked to the quality of the final object.

In practical terms, process parameters influence bonding and quality by affecting:
- the precision of the cut [N7-R5],
- the adhesion between layers [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R4],
- the surface roughness and dimensional accuracy [N7-R1][N5-R2],
- the thermal and mechanical behavior of the material [N7-R4],
- and the overall efficiency and cycle time [N7-R2][N7-R3].

The evidence is strongest on the basic principle of sheet cutting and bonding, while the process-parameter details are more indirect and mostly indicate that they are important but not fully detailed in the provided sources [N1-R1][N1-F1][N7-R5].

Practical implementation and technical considerations

Equipment and tool selection for LOM
LOM equipment and tool selection depend on the process flow: feeding, cutting, bonding, and post-processing. The evidence shows that the process uses a supply roll, a stage, a mechanical cutter or laser, a heat roller, and a waste roll [N1-F1][N2-R2]. A laser is explicitly mentioned as the cutting tool in several sources, including the statement that the first step is the lamination of sheet material and the second step is the cutting of that material with a computer-controlled laser [N2-R4]. Another source says that successive layers are cut precisely using a mechanical cutter or laser [N2-R2]. This means that the choice of cutting tool is central to the process, with lasers being a common but not exclusive option [N2-R2][N2-R4].

For bonding, the sources indicate that layers are either bonded together after cutting or fused with heat or adhesive [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The ScienceDirect overview says that successive layers are cut and then bonded together [N1-F1], while another source states that the cut layers are then fused together using heat or adhesive [N1-R1]. This implies that bonding can be achieved through either thermal or adhesive means, depending on the material and the desired final properties [N1-R1][N1-F1].

The evidence also suggests the importance of a heat roller in the process, as ScienceDirect describes the printing cycle as involving rolling out a heat-activated sheet material and laminating it onto a substrate via the heat roller [N1-F1]. This means that the heat roller is part of the equipment selection and can affect material handling and lamination quality [N1-F1].

Process parameters that affect quality and speed
Several process parameters are identified as affecting quality and speed. The ScienceDirect overview states that optimized laser power and scanning speed are key process parameters in the LOM technique [N7-R5]. Another source reports that an experimental investigation examined the influence of different process parameters on the vertical surfaces of LOM parts, measuring surface roughness [N7-R1]. A critical review says that process parameters such as roller speed, roller temperature, laser cutting, and other variables affect the process [N7-R2][N7-R3]. A thermomechanical analysis notes that process parameters such as roller temperature, velocity, indentation, and chamber air temperature affect temperature and stress distributions [N7-R4].

These parameters influence the final object in several ways:
- laser power and scanning speed affect cutting quality and bonding [N7-R5].
- roller speed and temperature affect the lamination and adhesion process [N7-R2][N7-R3][N7-R4].
- chamber air temperature and base plate temperature affect thermal behavior and dimensional stability [N7-R3][N7-R4].
- indentation and other mechanical parameters affect stress and deformation [N7-R4].

Material compatibility and process constraints
Material compatibility is a major technical consideration. The sources indicate that LOM can use a variety of materials such as paper, plastics, metals, ceramics, and composite prepregs [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-F2]. However, the same sources also show that metal LOM has special constraints. One source states that metal sheet lamination, known as LOM, is a relatively inexpensive 3D printing technique for metallic and ceramic materials [N3-R1]. Another source says that metal sheet lamination is used for functional metal parts, and that metal parts can be manufactured rapidly using 1.0 mm thick sheet metal [N3-F2]. The study also notes that the modeling accuracy is mainly affected by the sheet thickness, with thinner sheets generally yielding higher accuracy [N3-F2].

Process constraints include:
- the thickness of the sheet material [N3-F2],
- the choice of bonding method (adhesive, heat, or diffusion welding) [N1-R1][N1-F1][N3-F2],
- the need for post-processing to improve surface finish and dimensional accuracy [N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R3],
- the time required to remove excess material and support structures [N1-F1],
- and the compatibility of the chosen material with the cutting and bonding process [N1-F1][N3-F2].

Dimensional accuracy and surface finish issues
Dimensional accuracy is a limitation of LOM. ScienceDirect explicitly states that LOM has poor to average finish and that its dimensional accuracy is lower compared to the powder-bed methods [N1-F1]. It also says that the accuracy of the z-axis is dependent on the thickness of the sheet used and the adhesion pressure [N1-F1]. The same source notes that the theoretical error in LOM arises from the step between each slice of sheet and the modeling surface, and that this step must be removed by finish processing [N1-F1].

Surface finish issues are addressed through post-processing. Multiple sources indicate that post-processing can improve surface finish and dimensional accuracy [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Specific post-processing methods cited in the evidence include immersion, vapor treatment, polishing, and other finishing techniques [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The evidence also suggests that post-processing is especially important for improving the final appearance and dimensional accuracy of LOM parts [N5-R2][N5-R3].

Overall, the technical considerations are clear: LOM requires careful selection of equipment and tools, including a cutting system, heat roller, and bonding method; it is sensitive to process parameters such as laser power, roller speed, and temperature; it is compatible with a wide range of materials but has special constraints when using metal or ceramic sheets; and it relies on post-processing to address surface finish and dimensional accuracy limitations [N1-F1][N2-R2][N7-R5][N5-R2][N5-R3].

Bonding, adhesion, and support-structure behavior

Mechanisms of layer adhesion and bonding
The evidence indicates that layer adhesion and bonding are central to LOM and that they can be achieved through several mechanisms. The ScienceDirect overview states that successive layers are cut and then bonded together either by forming then bonding or bonding then forming [N1-F1]. Another source says that the cut layers are then fused together using heat or adhesive [N1-R1]. This means that LOM bonding is not limited to a single mechanism; it can involve both thermal and adhesive bonding, depending on the material and the process configuration [N1-R1][N1-F1].

The mechanism of adhesion is also described in general adhesion theory. ScienceDirect states that adhesion can be summarized as mechanical interlocking, intermolecular bonding, chain entanglement, diffusion, and electrostatic binding [N4-R4]. A more detailed review explains that adhesion processes are complex and that adhesion can be formed by primary and secondary forces, including primary chemical forces such as ionic, covalent, and metallic bonds and secondary physical forces such as dipole-dipole interactions, London dispersion, and van der Waals forces [N4-F3]. The review also notes that primary bonds are stronger than secondary bonds, and that specific surface pretreatment is often needed to achieve stronger interaction [N4-F3]. It further states that covalent bonds are the most common primary bonds and that adhesion can be modified chemically by incorporating functional groups or using coupling agents and adhesion promoters [N4-F3].

Support-structure adhesion issues and design considerations
Support-structure adhesion issues are relevant in LOM, even though the evidence here is more general than LOM-specific. One source discusses support structure adhesion issues in 3D printing and notes that support structures may not adhere properly [N4-R1]. Another source describes first-layer adhesion issues for support material, indicating that support material can fail to adhere at the first layer [N4-R2]. These sources suggest that support-structure adhesion is a common concern in additive manufacturing, but they do not provide a detailed LOM-specific design methodology.

In the context of LOM, support structures are created from the same or compatible sheet material and are later removed [N1-F1]. The evidence indicates that excess material after cutting is left for the support, and after completion of the process, it can be removed and recycled [N1-F1]. This implies that support structures are part of the build process and are designed to hold up overhanging or complex regions during printing [N1-F1]. However, the provided evidence does not detail how they are specifically designed or how adhesion between the support and the object is optimized [N4-R1][N4-R2].

Conditions that cause delamination or poor bonding
Delamination or poor bonding can occur when the adhesion conditions are not favorable. The adhesion review states that adhesion can fail if the interface is not intimate enough, if the contact area is insufficient, or if the bond is not strong enough [N4-F3]. It also notes that wetting is strongly related to adhesion and that the surface energy of the adherent should be higher than the surface energy of the adhesive for effective wetting [N4-F3]. Poor bonding may therefore result from:
- insufficient intimacy or contact area,
